column3: Cybersecurity career module includes risks and ethics; guided labs do not establish agent supervision or code-analysis harness design.
Published workshop includes AI-use policy, measuring projects and roadmap activity; generic leadership material does not teach agent autonomy controls.
Current MIT page includes shadow-AI exposure and workforce awareness. General audits do not demonstrate agent-control assurance.
Session titles introduce workflows, strategy, impact and governance; no detailed agent or cyber curriculum.
Provider page still blocked by a robot check; course title alone cannot support numerical teaching assessments.
NUS topic list names AI threat modelling, exploitation and mitigations; depth beyond headings is not public.
Development-stage outline names AI defence, threats, governance and strategy; no teaching depth or practice is evidenced.
Only the announcement for this self-paced course supports assessment; do not transfer the detailed VERIFY/FEAT syllabus from the distinct in-person IBFAILF course.
Path modules include supply-chain attacks and malicious MCP servers. Generic ML model building is not agent engineering or operator evaluation.
Exam-only; preserve objective mapping separately from teaching evidence.
Benchmarking infrastructure with no published learner curriculum; resource availability is not teaching coverage.
AI forensics is only named; supply-chain security is a taught module. No agent forensic readiness or evidence-preservation method is evidenced.
Defender workflow examples and responsible-use introduction; demonstrations do not evidence complete oversight practice.
Defence episode introduces guardrails; PyRIT datasets and scorers introduce security-evaluation components, without a complete operator evaluation method.
Crescendo challenges demonstrate guardrail evasion, but not guardrail engineering as a whole.
Runnable attack datasets and scoring workflows teach partial test design and checks. Model-based scorers are not evidence of validation against human labels.
Failure-mode mitigations cover consent fatigue, inter-agent trust, tool controls and supply-chain validation. Reading-only; no full operational sign-off.
Agent registry, identity, tool restrictions, monitoring and disablement guidance support partial controls. Forensic logging is mentioned without integrity/reconstruction detail.
SAIF agent guidance covers least privilege, consequential-action approval, auditable tool use and risk self-assessment; no practical supervision assessment.
Day-four quality codelabs include traces, metrics and evaluation of responses/tool use. Human approval is introduced with tools, not full oversight training.
Responsible-use module and human-oversight outcomes support basic diligence and awareness; no bank-specific handling rules.
AITECH published objectives explicitly introduce HITL, MCP primitives, agent design and workflow optimisation; topic names do not evidence the corresponding advanced skills.
Cisco tutorial description names adversarial threats, OWASP, ATLAS and model defences; product marketing is excluded from teaching evidence.
Scanner documentation explains probes, detectors and result reports. It supplies model-security checks, not general agent evaluations or a curriculum.
Published 4D curriculum supports existing mappings. Platform privacy FAQs are not learning content and do not create N4 coverage.
Team roles, gradual release and information boundaries introduce delegation and autonomy; surrounding Academy course advertisements excluded.
MCP tools, roots boundaries and logging notifications are introduced; no authorisation/connector-vetting method. Other courses on the catalogue landing page excluded.
Course roadmap explicitly mentions future authentication/authorisation. This is awareness, not implemented security practice.
Official announcement names boundaries and reviewing results, but no detailed supervision curriculum is published.
Leadership outcomes include ownership/governance of initiatives; surrounding Academy builder-course content excluded.

Evaluation/error-analysis module teaches test examples, component diagnosis and performance metrics. It does not validate judges against human labels or aggregate a whole domain's practitioner results.
Manual and automated chatbot testing contributes test design and checks; benchmarking discussion and model-based evaluators remain partial.
Agent construction and tracing labs were omitted from the prior needs list. Judge improvement and production monitoring are introductory; no complete human-label validation method is established.
Input/output guard labs include confidentiality and PII; probabilistic outputs are explicitly introduced. No prompt-injection defence inferred.
Brief extensions/security lesson mentions protocol security; no full identity or authorisation engineering practice.
Bonus observability/evaluation unit adds traces, offline benchmarks and online judges. Monitoring does not imply kill switches or validated automated judges.
Lectures on evaluation and safety introduce relevant concepts; research talks and optional projects do not establish a complete operational curriculum.
Available early builder slides cover context, grounding and tools; later safety topics are scheduled headings only. Enrolled-student labs are not attributed to the public-materials record.
Frontier-model alignment, evaluations and defence research are adjacent introductions, not agent operating skills.
System-card interpretation and policy briefings are transferable awareness only; the provider explicitly excludes corporate compliance.
Inspect tutorials document agent traces, sandboxes and tool-approval controls. Release-note bug fixes are not treated as additional taught topics.
2026 mitigations cover deterministic authorisation, scoped tool calls, MCP signing/pinning and retrieval logs. These are partial reading-based controls, not bank operating practice.
Agentic Top 10 mitigations include approval, trust abuse, bounded identity, supply chain and rogue-agent containment; no exercises or complete incident playbooks.
Architecture and threat taxonomy explain agent patterns, cross-agent attacks, HITL overload and signed component provenance. Knowledge reference only.
Guardian lifecycle hooks, action audit and AgBOM support partial inventory/control-assurance learning. Early specification and conformance checks are not learner exercises.
Report sections cover agent identity, provenance and regulation. Content from other reports advertised on the OWASP landing page is excluded.
Red-team blueprint, test datasets, metrics and continuous testing support security-specific evaluation. No general domain evaluation or human-label calibration is inferred.
Published test cases include expected results, remediation, delegated identity and permission abuse. Reading-only test library, not completed practice.
CTF demonstrates policy bypass and MCP/tool poisoning. Platform implementation features and roadmap attacks are not credited as learner instruction.
ATLAS techniques/cases explicitly cover indirect injection, agent tool supply-chain compromise and rug pulls; references do not teach the exposure-management lifecycle.
GenAI Profile describes AI-enabled threats and suggested measurement/monitoring actions. Workforce effects are acknowledged, not a junior-pipeline design method.
Taxonomy includes multimodal models and generative-AI supply-chain attacks. Poison forensics is not forensic readiness for agent traces.
Draft profile names guardrails, fallback, AI component inventories and least privilege. CSF outcome statements are not a detailed method or practice.
NICE knowledge/skill statements are a workforce taxonomy, not lessons. Their topic names are not credited as teaching.
Joint guidance describes distinct agent identities, time-bounded access, protected logs, graduated autonomy and rollback. Reading-only; bank execution and drill details remain gaps.

Current guideline text gives concrete third-party due diligence, import isolation and monitoring recommendations. Pre-agentic scope limits the coverage but does not justify suppressing these partial requirements.
Code provisions cover supply-chain control, human oversight, asset inventories and audit records; generic AI lifecycle provisions are not full agent controls.
ANSSI recommendations explain hallucination/injection, restricted-data hosting and third-party solutions. Bank-specific classifications still require internal completion.
Available agency summary supports critical review and local handling of code. Full PDF remains unavailable; no further technical depth inferred.
CERT-FR bulletin names sandboxing, restricted tool access and human approval. Short recommendations provide awareness rather than operational training.
Companion guide gives injection and supply-chain controls with worked cases; pre-agentic forensic and access-control references do not satisfy agent-specialist requirements.
Agentic addendum provides concrete architecture, identity, logging, containment and human-control guidance with cases. Reading-only; not an operational drill or complete specialist curriculum.
Older multilayer framework names AI threats, supply chain and risk practices. Historic regulatory discussion is not current compliance training.

Landing page now explains the Article 4 literacy duty and limitations of copying practices; regional regulator expectations are still absent. Repository is programme-design reference, not a learner course.
Published category/test summaries include control hijacking, trace evasion and accountability checks. Separate technical-implementation documents linked on the page are excluded.
Autonomy proposal explains enforceable boundaries and approval levels. It remains a proposed framework, not a standard or practical course.
Prototype landing page describes AI's effect on roles; security-specific entries are not visible.
Hub paper titles indicate relevant topics only. Membership papers have not been inferred from titles.
Interactive prompt-attacking game supports awareness; dynamically rendered challenge detail is unavailable.
Web LLM lesson gives access-control and output-validation defences alongside labs; no MCP or whole-agent control plane inferred.
Competition/tutorial explicitly concerns attacks on AI; specialised non-cyber challenge tracks excluded.
Chatbot challenges expose prompt-driven authentication bypass without teaching a secure authorisation design.
Password-extraction game is introductory direct-injection practice; no current detailed syllabus retrievable.
ReAct banking lab reveals tool access-control abuse; operating the supplied lab is not agent-building training.
MCP challenges demonstrate scopes, tool poisoning and rug pulls. They do not teach a discovery, hash-approval or scanning programme.
Agent red-team guide includes trace-based tests and reusable trajectory assertions. Product navigation and unrelated plug-ins are not added as course content.
Community/events index signals current AI attacks, without a stable assessable curriculum.
Four-properties lessons support the existing limitation mappings; lesson text is gated and platform privacy FAQs are excluded.
Teaching/assessment of human AI fluency may support internal trainers. Assessing students is not N9/N11 evaluation of AI systems.

Current published topic detail includes fail-closed controls, parameter validation, review gates and safe logging. Detailed course/lab content remains behind login, so no full-practice scores are inferred.
Official path now includes governance/risk/compliance. Four course outlines cover risk frameworks, vendor risk, monitoring/audit and AI workflow automation; video-only evidence caps skills below 3.

Current LDR553 outline explicitly addresses hallucination, human accountability, restraint and evidence preservation in agent incidents. Generic human-account revocation is not scored as agent IAM training.
SOC syllabus has a workflow-risk-assessment lab, agent configuration and approval/audit controls. SOC use does not imply agent incident response or code-analysis harness capability.
Databricks walkthroughs teach distinct identity, least-privilege data access and tracing. Product-specific demonstrations are partial skills coverage, not complete bank governance.
Public collection descriptions name evaluations, RBAC, guardrails and observability. Individual lab detail is gated; no deeper claims inferred.
Workshop titles introduce MCP and agent security; other resources on the learning hub are excluded.
AIMS certification outline names performance evaluation and responsible management; it does not evidence agent-control auditing or production drift measurement methods.
Enterprise governance lessons explain identity, execution containment, policy control and inventory through Microsoft examples. No full operational IAM lifecycle.
Security-controls module introduces content filters, monitoring and library review. Model/app controls remain partial for agents.
Maturity guidance includes ownership, registry and telemetry; a maturity checklist is not a control-testing course.
Prompt-injection awareness is present; leader tabletop exercises do not establish technical red-teaming competence.
Detailed security-engineering modules also teach supply-chain risk, safe connector use and deployment controls. Short lab videos are not assumed to be hands-on learner assessments.
Coding-agent framework explicitly treats untrusted input, hallucinated packages, consent fatigue, MCP permissions and staged approvals. Reading-only and coding-specific.
Skills-risk document includes malicious instructions, component inventories and installation governance. Draft mitigations are not a complete Skills-library implementation course.
